messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 53-year-old social worker from North America, has been grappling with the aftermath of a sexual assault that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event left an indelible mark on his psyche, and he now finds himself experiencing intense shame and terror whenever he recalls it. Each memory dredges up not just the physical pain but also the overwhelming sense of violation. "When I remember what happened," Mark admits, "the same terror floods me as if it were happening all over again." This fear is compounded by a profound feeling of shame that silences him; he knows what transpired but struggles to articulate his experience. The memory of the assault has fueled several maladaptive strategies in Mark's life. Most notably, he has started avoiding enclosed spaces and rumination about revenge. "I try not to be in small rooms or confined areas," he explains. "It feels like I can't escape if something goes wrong." This avoidance is driven by a deep-seated belief that being trapped will make him vulnerable again. Moreover, the thoughts of how to get even with his assailant consume much of his waking hours. The more he ruminates on revenge, the more entrenched his fear and anxiety become. Mark's threat perceptions are also heightened by his memories. Each time he remembers the assault, the terror is so intense that it triggers a persistent sense of danger in his daily life. "I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me," Mark confesses. This hyper-vigilance extends to avoiding unfamiliar places because he cannot assess their safety. The unpredictability of new environments exacerbates his fears, leading him to assume something bad is happening when delays occur. His avoidance behaviors have further reinforced his threat perceptions. For instance, whenever he steps into a crowded room or an enclosed space at work, the memory of the assault floods back with intense shame and terror. "I push those thoughts out of my mind," Mark says, acknowledging his efforts to suppress them. Yet, this suppression only serves to heighten his anxiety about potential threats. He believes that any delay in his daily routine could mean something is wrong, leading him to constantly monitor for signs of danger. Mark's avoidance has also strained his relationships with colleagues at work. His need to avoid enclosed spaces often means he misses important meetings or has to leave early. "I know it looks like I’m not taking my responsibilities seriously," Mark admits, feeling the weight of these actions on his professional life. Despite this awareness, he cannot shake off the pervasive fear that something bad will happen if he does not stick closely to familiar environments. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a particularly harrowing incident at work. During a mandatory meeting in an enclosed conference room, the memories overwhelmed him and he had to leave abruptly, leading to significant embarrassment and concern from his supervisor. "I’m afraid of becoming someone I don’t recognize," Mark says with a mixture of resignation and hope. He is desperate for relief from these overwhelming thoughts and fears that have taken over his life. In therapy, Mark hopes to find ways to process the memories without falling into cycles of avoidance and rumination. What frightens him most is the thought of never fully recovering and continuing to live in constant fear. His primary goal is to regain a sense of control and peace, so he can return to living a fulfilling life as a social worker and a husband.
